opus-5.5.text:
I have a lot of respect for what Generalist has been doing. They've taken pretraining seriously: collecting large amounts of real-world physical interaction data and actually measuring how performance scales with it. For a long time robotics didn't have that discipline. People trained a model for one task and one setup, then started over. So showing that there may be scaling behavior in embodied data is an important signal for the whole field.

Where I see things a bit differently is in what we mean by a "native" robot brain. Much of the current wave, including very good work, still inherits its structure from language or vision-language models: pretrain a big backbone, then attach an action head or map actions into tokens. That's a practical starting point, but I don't think it's the end state. A robot doesn't experience the world as text, or even as a sequence of images. It experiences continuous, physical, causal dynamics. It acts, the world responds, and it has to anticipate that response.

So for me the core question isn't only "how much data can we pretrain on?" It's "what is the right thing to learn during pretraining?" I believe a native robot brain should, from the beginning, model how the world evolves and how its own actions change it. That makes it closer to a world model with action built in than to a perception model with action bolted on. Data is still critical, but the objective and the representation matter just as much.

I'd say our approaches are complementary rather than opposed. Their results on data scale tell us the fuel is worth collecting. What we're trying to figure out is what kind of engine burns that fuel most efficiently for physical intelligence. If those two lines of work meet, I think the field moves much faster than people expect.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts native world modeling with language or vision-language backbones and bolted-on action heads, but does not say that Shen has not seen others make video generation native to a robot brain as his team proposes.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Generalist's work is actually quite encouraging, and in many ways it validates a direction we've believed in for a long time. The core idea is the same: the robot brain shouldn't be stitched together from separately trained modules, with a vision model here, a language model there, and a control policy bolted on at the end. It should be one model that learns perception, reasoning, and action jointly, at scale, the way foundation models in language and vision learned.

Where they've done something important is in showing that scaling laws seem to hold for embodied data. When they push the amount of manipulation data up by orders of magnitude, performance keeps improving in a fairly predictable way. That was not obvious a couple of years ago. A lot of people in robotics assumed data for embodied tasks was too heterogeneous, too noisy, too tied to a specific hardware setup, for scaling to work the way it did for text. Their result gives the whole field more confidence to invest in data at that scale.

Where our thinking differs is more on what "native" means. For me, a native robot brain isn't just a large model trained on a large pile of trajectories. It's a model whose training objective is grounded in the physical world from the start. Language and vision pretraining give you a lot of prior knowledge about the world, but they give you very little about contact, force, latency, or what happens when you push on something and it doesn't move. So we spend a lot of effort on how the model represents actions, how it handles time, and how it learns from interaction and failure, rather than only from demonstrations.

The other thing I'd say is that pretraining is really only half of the problem. The hardest question is how you close the loop between the model and the real world. A model that has seen tens of thousands of hours of manipulation video still has to deal with the fact that its own actions change what it sees next. So we think a lot about post-training, about on-robot learning, about how to make the system improve from its own deployment rather than only from human-collected data.

So I'd say we're climbing the same mountain. Generalist has shown that the data path is real and that scaling works. Our bet is on making the model's structure and learning process more deeply embodied, so that when the data arrives, the model is actually built to use it. I think the two approaches will converge, and honestly I hope they do, because the field moves faster when several groups are pushing on the same core hypothesis from different angles.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from video and embodied interaction, but does not say the brain must learn knowledge through video generation.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that others have failed to make video generation native to a robot brain.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame the relationship in terms of what we want pretraining to accomplish. For a native robot brain, the goal is to learn representations that connect perception, action, and the consequences of action. The robot needs to understand the world through its ability to interact with it.

From that perspective, Generalist’s pretraining work and our approach address a shared question: how much of a robot’s capability can come from a foundation that transfers across tasks? The distinction I would want to explore is what that foundation learns. Does it mainly provide a useful starting point for learning individual skills, or does it develop an understanding that lets the robot adapt when the task or environment changes?

That’s the standard I’d use to judge progress toward a native robot brain: how much the robot can carry into a new situation, and how little additional teaching it needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as exploring a very related question: how do we use pretraining to give robots capabilities that transfer across tasks, rather than training a separate policy for every task? That direction is very much aligned with the idea of a native robot brain.

For me, the key question is what the model learns during pretraining. Recognizing objects or understanding an instruction is part of it, but a robot also needs to learn how its actions change the world, and how to use feedback when things don’t go as expected. So I’d look at Generalist’s work through that lens: how much of the pretrained capability translates into robust physical behavior, and how efficiently can it adapt to a new task or environment?

I wouldn’t draw a sharp distinction without knowing more about their approach. Pretraining can be a foundation for a native robot brain. The challenge is connecting that foundation to perception, action, and learning in the physical world.
